title: Balancing Innovation and Impact: Assessing Post-Pandemic EdTech -future-96a99d09f2a1
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Writing five years after the pandemic lockdowns, Andrew Marcinek reviews what remote learning exposed: unequal access to devices and connectivity, the absence of a digital health and wellness plan, and a scramble to adapt teaching to virtual settings. He argues that schools threw strategic technology planning aside during and after the pandemic and should now treat the moment as a period to pause and reflect. He proposes three conversations every school should have before the next school year: reexamining the technology ecosystem and the return on 1:1 devices, checking equity of access beyond school hours, and giving teachers real instructional-design support with technology. The central claim is that technology decisions in schools need to be intentional rather than inherited from emergency measures. The piece is a school-policy argument about ed-tech itself, so it belongs in Ed-Tech.
points: Marcinek argues that 1:1 device programs adopted as pandemic emergency measures should be re-evaluated for return on investment, with some K-6 schools pulling back to classroom sets.
Technology can widen inequity when students can only reach digital resources during school hours, so access at home should be reviewed yearly.
Teacher support with technology should mean instructional design that elevates learning, not handing over a device and a login.
He frames the present as a Great Pause and Reflect period in which schools should ask why and how they use technology.
quotes: During, and after the pandemic we threw strategic, intentional technology planning and implementation by the wayside. It’s time that schools pause, and begin conversations about why and how technology is used in classrooms.

After the pandemic, students K-12 returned with devices and more bad habits around screens than prior to the pandemic. What’s more, many of the devices purchased during the pandemic are aging out and school budgets are getting squeezed with trying to replace and refresh these devices. Schools need to make efforts to strategically redesign their educational device plan. In some cases, it makes sense to pull back the 1:1 model and repurpose devices in classroom sets. Especially in grades K-6. We need to get back to basics in school and really interrogate the ROI on a 1:1 device implementation.

While I strongly believe technology is a great leveler for equity, it can also, in some cases, create greate inequity if students can only access digital resources when they are within the hours of school.

By this I simply don’t mean hand them a device and make sure they know their login information and passwords for apps. No. What I mean is true instructional design with technology to support and elevate student learning and engagement.

One of the most pressing concerns was ensuring that all students had equitable access to technology and a stable internet connection. While some students had access to multiple devices and reliable networks at home, others faced significant barriers. This digital divide exacerbated existing inequities in education, as students from disadvantaged backgrounds struggled to keep up with their peers.

Another challenge was the need for a comprehensive digital health and wellness plan. With students spending extended periods of time in front of screens, concerns about the impact on their physical and mental well-being arose. The absence of clear guidelines and protocols to mitigate the risks associated with excessive screen time left many educators and parents overwhelmed.
